classification.tone: Grounded, wistful, lightly comedic, emotionally reflective

evaluation.positioning_hook: A suburban executive wakes up with ten years missing and must rebuild his marriage, career, and conscience before the truth he forgot catches up to him.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to grasp and emotionally legible: a man loses a decade and has to face the life he built in the gap. The audience lane is clear, though this plays more as an adult character drama than a broad four-quadrant commercial swing.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages with Tim waking up in 2009 while still mentally living in 1999. The story engine stays clean through the doctor visits, the library assignment, and the final reveal that his memory loss is tied to a hit-and-run.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Tim has a strong central contradiction: polished partner on the outside, disoriented and morally unsettled on the inside. Nancy, Steve, Jean, and Josh each give him a different pressure point, though the script is still most alive through Tim rather than through a deeply layered ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The time-gap amnesia angle is familiar, but the script gives it a domestic, middle-aged, corporate-suburban texture that feels specific. The choice to make the mystery about a buried accident and a lost decade of emotional drift gives it a more personal shape than a standard memory-thriller setup.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps moving through a sequence of discoveries: the changed home, the office, the doctor, the psychologist, the library, and the final memory trigger. The momentum is steady and readable, with the strongest propulsion coming from each new layer of what Tim does not know about his own life.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a man discovering he has emotionally and morally disappeared from his own life has a strong aftertaste. The final reveal that the missing decade is tied to a child’s bicycle accident gives the premise a tragic inevitability that helps it land.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The suburban home, corporate office, valet, doctor’s office, and library all carry recognizable texture from the late-90s/2009 contrast. The world is specific enough to support the premise, though it functions more as a believable container than as a fully generative ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends deadpan workplace comedy, marital friction, and quiet existential unease in a way that feels consistent. The script’s best tonal move is letting Tim’s confusion play against everyone else’s casual acceptance, which creates a distinct, rueful flavor.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the amnesia premise sits a story about emotional absence, marriage fatigue, and the cost of self-erasure. The final memory of the bicycle accident suggests there is more moral weight under the surface than the early scenes initially advertise.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Tim and Nancy carry the emotional spine, with Steve, Jean, Josh, and the adult children adding useful pressure and contrast. The relationships are functional and often amusing, though the script still lives primarily on the lead’s perspective rather than on a web of equally active dynamics.

casting_characteristics: One child role in the opening timeline
Adult versions of children in the present timeline

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with some exterior driving and street scenes

technical.vfx_details: No visible VFX requirements beyond simple title/date inserts and period dressing.
technical.sfx_needs: A bicycle impact and a low-speed vehicle backing incident are the main practical action beats.

rights_flags.detail: Oldies 104.7, XM station references, and named sports/music/pop-culture references may require clearances depending on production use

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature or prestige cable-style theatrical indie
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Festival-to-platform or limited theatrical with strong adult-drama positioning

cost.note: Contemporary, dialogue-driven, and largely contained to homes, offices, a bar, a clinic, and a library.

cast.note: The lead is central, but the script depends on a solid supporting ensemble and age-specific casting across the 1999 and 2009 timelines.

location.note: About ten distinct locations with several company moves, plus driving scenes and a period-shifted opening sequence.

content.note: The material is emotionally mature but avoids explicit violence, sex, or heavy language beyond a few sharp exchanges.

rights.note: The script names multiple brands, real people, sports figures, and pop-culture references throughout the dialogue and scene texture.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the engine in one sentence: a man wakes up ten years out of sync with his own life and has to reconstruct the truth before it reconstructs him. That clarity makes it easy to market to adult audiences who respond to mystery with emotional stakes, not just puzzle-box mechanics.
strengths.evidence: The opening shift from 1999 to 2009, Tim’s panic in the bathroom mirror, and the newspaper date establish the hook immediately.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Tim is built for a lead actor.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives an actor a playable contradiction: confident executive, baffled husband, and man slowly realizing he may have become someone he doesn’t respect. That kind of part attracts mid-career dramatic leads looking for a showcase that can carry both comedy and ache.
strengths.evidence: Tim’s deadpan office authority, his confusion with modern objects, and his emotional unraveling in the doctor’s office all sit on the same character.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The marriage is the emotional engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has a built-in adult relationship spine, which gives the project more staying power than a pure memory mystery. That makes it attractive to buyers who want a thriller premise with a human center and to actors who want scenes that play opposite a strong female lead.
strengths.evidence: The kitchen-table confrontation with Nancy, the spare-room dynamic, and the late reveal that she has been carrying the marriage for years.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The office world has comic texture.
strengths.what_it_means: The corporate setting gives the script a steady stream of behavior-based comedy without undercutting the drama, which broadens the audience beyond straight genre buyers. Directors and buyers who like workplace satire inside a serious frame will see a clean tonal lane here.
strengths.evidence: Randy the valet, Jean’s no-nonsense authority, Steve’s office loitering, and Tim’s baffled return to his own corner office.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending re-frames the whole story.
strengths.what_it_means: The final bicycle accident reveal turns the amnesia from a quirky premise into a moral wound, which gives the script a stronger aftertaste and a more memorable final note. That kind of reveal helps a producer sell the script as more than a gimmick and gives audiences a reason to talk about it after the credits.
strengths.evidence: The flashback to the parking lot, the SUV backing into the child, and the final fade out.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, adult-facing feature with a strong hook, a playable lead role, and a marriage story hiding inside a memory mystery. It has the kind of contained footprint and emotional clarity that can travel well with the right cast, while the final reveal gives the whole piece a sharper moral edge than the premise first suggests.

lead_characters.name: Tim Sullivan
lead_characters.hook: A polished suburban partner who wakes up mentally trapped in 1999 and has to navigate a 2009 life he helped build but no longer recognizes. He’s funny, vain, defensive, and gradually heartbreaking as the script strips away the confidence and leaves him with the question of who he became while he was gone.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Keaton in Birdman or Hugh Grant in a more grounded dramatic register — a man whose charm is inseparable from self-deception, and whose unraveling has to stay funny even when it hurts. Actors who want a role that lets them play denial, comic confusion, and late-blooming remorse in the same frame will chase this.

lead_characters.name: Nancy Sullivan
lead_characters.hook: Nancy is the emotional adult in the room, a wife who has learned how to live beside a man who is physically present but often elsewhere. She carries hurt with discipline, flashes of wit, and just enough tenderness to make the marriage feel worth saving.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, emotionally exacting role Laura Linney or Toni Collette has made a calling card — a woman whose restraint is the performance, and whose pain lands because she refuses to perform it for the room. Prestige-drama actresses looking for a marriage role with real interior life will see immediate value here.

lead_characters.name: Steve Johnson
lead_characters.hook: Tim’s best friend is a loud, drinking, sexually unfiltered corporate insider who knows exactly how the old world works and has no interest in pretending otherwise. He’s comic relief with teeth, but he also functions as the keeper of the script’s buried history.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing support that made Philip Seymour Hoffman or Paul Giamatti so magnetic in ensemble dramas — a role that can steal scenes with rhythm, then turn and deliver the truth the lead can’t say out loud. Character actors who want a big, quotable, high-utility part will line up for it.

lead_characters.name: Jean Gordon
lead_characters.hook: Jean is Tim’s long-time assistant, the only person in the office who can puncture his status without fear. She’s efficient, dry, and quietly affectionate, with the kind of institutional memory that makes her feel indispensable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role Frances McDormand or Allison Janney can turn into a stealth centerpiece — a supporting part whose authority comes from precision, not volume. Veteran actresses who like playing the smartest person in the room will be drawn to her.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Josh Strasberg
lead_characters.hook: Josh is the low-key psychologist who becomes the script’s guide through memory, denial, and emotional avoidance. He’s patient, slightly amused by his own profession, and able to shift from comic deadpan to genuine concern without changing his temperature much.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of calm, intelligent support that made roles for actors like Richard Jenkins or David Strathairn so appealing — a man whose stillness becomes the frame for someone else’s crisis. Actors who want to play authority without bluster will respond to it.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Sullivan
lead_characters.demographics: Male · 10 in the opening timeline; early 20s in the present timeline
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is first the kid Tim half-recognizes, then the adult son who has learned to read his father’s moods with practiced speed. He’s dry, observant, and more emotionally fluent than Tim expects, which gives him a quiet authority in the family scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of age-spanning family role that lets an actor play innocence and maturity in one package, similar to the emotional range seen in coming-of-age family dramas where the child later becomes the adult witness. Younger actors who can handle both warmth and sarcasm will want it.

lead_characters.name: Julie Sullivan
lead_characters.demographics: Female · 15 in the opening timeline; mid-20s in the present timeline
lead_characters.hook: Julie starts as a sharp teenage daughter and becomes a composed adult daughter and mother who has inherited the family’s emotional habits. She’s affectionate, impatient, and just self-aware enough to see the pattern she grew up inside.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of daughter role that gives an actress a clean before-and-after arc, with the adult version carrying the authority of someone who has outgrown the parent-child dynamic. Performers who like playing intelligence with a little bite will gravitate to it.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Jones
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the son-in-law who arrives with domestic competence and a little too much confidence in the family system. He’s not flashy, but he gives the script a useful contrast to Tim’s stalled masculinity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean supporting husband role in the lane of the steady, grounded younger man — the kind of part that lets an actor play competence, mild irritation, and family belonging without needing a huge arc. Character actors who specialize in believable domestic realism will fit it well.

lead_characters.name: Jeremy
lead_characters.hook: Jeremy is the grandson who becomes a living marker of time passing, even when Tim can’t fully process it. He’s less a speaking engine than an emotional one, a reminder that the family has kept moving without him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but emotionally loaded child role that functions as the story’s proof of time. It’s the kind of part that matters because of what it represents, not because of dialogue.

lead_characters.name: Stan Gray
lead_characters.hook: Stan is the aggrieved business partner whose resentment has been simmering for years. He’s blustery, wounded, and just unstable enough to make the office politics feel personal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of combustible supporting role that lets an actor play grievance, humiliation, and status anxiety in one scene. Character actors who like playing men with a score to settle will see the juice immediately.

lead_characters.name: Stephanie Lorens
lead_characters.hook: Stephanie is the glamorous office affair who embodies the life Tim might have chosen if he had kept drifting. She’s seductive, self-possessed, and more emotionally aware than she first appears.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the classic adult-drama seductress role with a conscience, the kind of part that lets an actress play allure, disappointment, and self-protection in the same scene. Performers who want a role with heat and subtext will be interested.

lead_characters.name: Randy
lead_characters.hook: Randy is the valet who knows Tim’s habits better than Tim does and isn’t impressed by the title. He’s funny, grounded, and one of the few people who can speak to Tim without deference.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, high-utility character part in the tradition of sharp working-class scene-stealers — the kind of role that gives an actor a memorable rhythm and a few great exchanges. Supporting players who can land comedy without broadening the movie will want it.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a midlife identity story feel like a mystery without losing the human ache.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with at least one or two character-driven features, or TV drama directors moving into features, who already work comfortably with performance-first material. The material rewards restraint, tonal control, and the ability to make office, home, and therapy scenes feel like escalating revelations rather than static dialogue scenes.
director_appeal.detail: The script gives a director a clean emotional spine, a contained footprint, and a final reveal that recontextualizes the whole movie. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who like adult behavior, dry humor, and the slow reveal of moral consequence.

buyer_appeal.detail: It can be packaged around one strong lead and a reliable supporting ensemble, so it doesn’t require a giant cast or effects spend to feel complete. The adult mystery lane and the marriage-centered emotional hook make it exportable to streamers and festival-to-platform buyers who want a contained, conversation-friendly feature.

considerations.area: The opening timeline can be even more surgical.
considerations.detail: The 1999 suburban routine is doing a lot of setup work at once — one next pass could consider compressing a few of the domestic beats so the time-jump surprise arrives with even more snap. The core idea is already clear, so the room is in how quickly the script gets from ordinary life to the first impossible detail.

considerations.area: The office and home scenes carry the same emotional job.
considerations.detail: Several conversations with Jean, Steve, and Nancy are all helping Tim discover that he has changed, which is useful, but a future pass could sharpen the distinction between each relationship’s job in the story. The version where each scene reveals a different facet of Tim — status, marriage, friendship, guilt — would make the middle feel even more cumulative.

considerations.area: The brand and pop-culture references are plentiful.
considerations.detail: The script leans on named products, sports figures, TV shows, and music cues to sell the time period and social texture. A production-minded pass could decide which of those references are essential to the joke or the memory trigger and which can be generalized without losing the scene’s flavor.

considerations.area: The final reveal is the script’s sharpest emotional lever.
considerations.detail: The bicycle accident lands with real force because it turns the memory gap into a moral event, not just a medical one. One direction would be to keep protecting that reveal’s emotional clarity so the audience feels the full weight of what Tim has been carrying without knowing it.
